summary: This standards-track document defines labels for Generalized MPLS to be used with lambda-switch-capable routers, which switch optical wavelengths. The labels identify specific wavelengths, so equipment from different vendors can agree on which one carries a given connection, including in flexible spacing of channels.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6205 defines a common way for GMPLS routers to name an optical wavelength. Network domains can use the same label fields to signal a wavelength across equipment from different vendors.

subtitle: A shared wavelength label format for optical switching across different network domains.

tldr.problem: Generalized MPLS wavelength labels were defined as meaningful only between neighboring routers, so different optical network domains lacked a shared wavelength representation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6205 defines a 32-bit wavelength label with fields for the grid, channel spacing, a per-node identifier and a signed value n. The fields identify a wavelength on either the ITU-T DWDM or CWDM grid.
tldr.outcome: The common label format supports wavelength information in GMPLS signaling and routing protocols. RFC 6205 updates RFC 3471 and is updated by RFC 7699 and RFC 8359.

today: RFC 6205 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It updates RFC 3471 and has been updated by RFC 7699 and RFC 8359.

sections.title: Why Optical Networks Need Shared Labels
sections.content:
Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) supports several kinds of switching, including Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) equipment that switches optical wavelengths. Earlier GMPLS signaling defined a wavelength label as significant only between two neighboring devices, without a common global wavelength meaning.

RFC 6205 defines a standard wavelength label based on the ITU-T Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) and Coarse Wavelength Division Multiplexing (CWDM) grids. A shared representation helps interoperate across domains using different optical equipment and avoids relying on each vendor's private label format.

The RFC describes a network where wavelength continuity may require one wavelength to be used across multiple domains. It notes that the way a constrained shortest path is calculated is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical equipment needs to agree on which wavelength a path will use. This RFC gives the equipment a shared label format instead of leaving each vendor to name wavelengths differently.

sections.title: Grid, Spacing and the Wavelength Value
sections.content:
The wavelength label identifies which grid applies, the channel spacing and a signed value called n. For DWDM, the frequency is calculated from 193.1 THz plus n times the channel spacing. The channel spacing values listed are 0.0125, 0.025, 0.05 and 0.1 THz. A wider spacing can be represented using a narrower spacing and a suitable value of n.

For CWDM, the wavelength is calculated from 1471 nm plus n times 20 nm. The value n is a two's-complement integer, so it can be positive, negative or zero. The RFC uses the grid and spacing rather than a channel index because the grids are not numbered and can change as technology advances.
sections.plainLanguage: The label says which wavelength grid and step size to use, then gives a signed count of steps from the grid's starting point. Together, those values identify the wavelength.

sections.title: The DWDM and CWDM Label Fields
sections.content:
Both wavelength-label formats use a 32-bit layout with four fields. Grid is 3 bits: value 1 means ITU-T DWDM and value 2 means ITU-T CWDM. Value 0 is reserved; values 3 through 7 are for future use.

Channel spacing is 4 bits. For DWDM, values 1, 2, 3 and 4 mean 100, 50, 25 and 12.5 GHz. For CWDM, value 1 means 20 nm. Zero is reserved in both, and the remaining values are reserved for future use according to each grid's table.

Identifier is 9 bits and distinguishes lasers in one node that can transmit the same frequency. A node may choose any value, including zero, and may change it per hop. Once selected for an LSP, the value must remain unchanged until the LSP is torn down and must be used in LSP-related messages. The final 16-bit field, n, is the signed value used in the frequency or wavelength calculation. In a label ERO subobject, zero lets the referenced node choose an identifier; a non-zero value must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has four fields: grid, spacing, a local laser identifier and the signed step count. The identifier helps distinguish lasers within one node, while the other fields identify the wavelength.

sections.title: Examples of the Two Grid Calculations
sections.content:
The DWDM example uses the ITU-T DWDM grid with 50 GHz channel spacing and a frequency of 193.35 THz. In the label, Grid is 1 and channel-spacing value is 2. Substituting the frequency and spacing into the RFC's formula gives n = 5.

The CWDM example uses the ITU-T CWDM grid, 20 nm channel spacing and a wavelength of 1331 nm. Grid is 2 and channel-spacing value is 1. Using the CWDM formula gives n = -7.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that the signed step count can move either upward or downward from the grid's starting value. One example uses DWDM; the other uses CWDM.

sections.title: Registries for Grid and Spacing Values
sections.content:
The RFC adds three subregistries to the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry: one for Grid values, one for DWDM channel spacing and one for CWDM channel spacing. Their initial entries include the grid codes and spacing codes defined by the label formats.

New values in each subregistry are assigned according to Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The three registries keep the official meanings of grid and spacing codes. A new code requires a Standards Action.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3471 and RFC 3473. It points to RFC 5920 for a general discussion of MPLS and GMPLS security.
sections.plainLanguage: This label format adds no new security concerns according to the RFC. It refers readers to the existing GMPLS security guidance.
